claim: Nicotine remains one of the most-widely used addictive substance in the world.
source: Nicotine remains one of the most-widely used addictive substance in the world, and even though cigarette smoking is overall decreasing, the use of new products such as electronic cigarettes has risen dramatically in recent years (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2021

claim: The use of electronic cigarettes has risen dramatically in recent years.
source: Nicotine remains one of the most-widely used addictive substance in the world, and even though cigarette smoking is overall decreasing, the use of new products such as electronic cigarettes has risen dramatically in recent years (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2021

claim: Nicotine administration induces a range of effects from pleasant to noxious.
source: Nicotine administration induces a range of effects, from pleasant (i.e. appetitive, rewarding, reinforcing, anxiolytic…) to noxious (i.e. anxiogenic, aversive…) (Fowler and Kenny, 2014; Verendeev and Riley, 2013; Wills et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fowler and Kenny, 2014; Verendeev and Riley, 2013; Wills et al., 2022

claim: The multifaceted effects of nicotine have been described both in humans and in rodents.
source: These multifaceted effects have been described both in humans and in rodents.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: The effects of nicotine greatly depend on the dose administered.
source: They greatly depend on the dose of nicotine administered, show substantial inter-individual variability, and are considered essential in the regulation of nicotine intake and in the maintenance of addiction.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: The effects of nicotine show substantial inter-individual variability.
source: They greatly depend on the dose of nicotine administered, show substantial inter-individual variability, and are considered essential in the regulation of nicotine intake and in the maintenance of addiction.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: The effects of nicotine are considered essential in the regulation of nicotine intake and in the maintenance of addiction.
source: They greatly depend on the dose of nicotine administered, show substantial inter-individual variability, and are considered essential in the regulation of nicotine intake and in the maintenance of addiction.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Nicotine mediates its physiological effects by activating nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs).
source: Nicotine mediates its physiological effects by activating nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), pentameric ligand-gated ion channels encoded by a large multigene family (Wills et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wills et al., 2022

claim: nAChRs are pentameric ligand-gated ion channels encoded by a large multigene family.
source: Nicotine mediates its physiological effects by activating nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), pentameric ligand-gated ion channels encoded by a large multigene family (Wills et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wills et al., 2022

claim: There are nine α (α2–10) and three β (β2–4) nAChR subunits expressed in the brain.
source: There are nine α (α2–10) and three β (β2–4) nAChR subunits expressed in the brain, which can assemble to form homo-pentamers or hetero-pentamers with various localizations and functions (Taly et al., 2009; Zoli et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taly et al., 2009; Zoli et al., 2015

claim: nAChR subunits can assemble to form homo-pentamers or hetero-pentamers with various localizations and functions.
source: There are nine α (α2–10) and three β (β2–4) nAChR subunits expressed in the brain, which can assemble to form homo-pentamers or hetero-pentamers with various localizations and functions (Taly et al., 2009; Zoli et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taly et al., 2009; Zoli et al., 2015

claim: Initiation of consumption and reinforcement to nicotine involve the mesolimbic dopamine reward circuit, which originates in the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: Initiation of consumption and reinforcement to nicotine involve the mesolimbic dopamine reward circuit, which originates in the ventral tegmental area (VTA; Maskos et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maskos et al., 2005

claim: Nicotine primarily acts on the mesolimbic dopamine reward circuit by activating α4β2 nAChRs.
source: Nicotine primarily acts on this circuit by activating α4β2 nAChRs, a receptor subtype that displays high affinity for the drug (Durand-de Cuttoli et al., 2018; Maskos et al., 2005; Tapper et al., 2004; Tolu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Durand-de Cuttoli et al., 2018; Maskos et al., 2005; Tapper et al., 2004; Tolu et al., 2013

claim: α4β2 nAChRs display high affinity for nicotine.
source: Nicotine primarily acts on this circuit by activating α4β2 nAChRs, a receptor subtype that displays high affinity for the drug (Durand-de Cuttoli et al., 2018; Maskos et al., 2005; Tapper et al., 2004; Tolu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Durand-de Cuttoli et al., 2018; Maskos et al., 2005; Tapper et al., 2004; Tolu et al., 2013

claim: An acute injection of nicotine inhibits a subset of VTA dopamine neurons that project to the amygdala.
source: An acute injection of nicotine also inhibits a subset of VTA dopamine neurons that project to the amygdala (Nguyen et al., 2021), and this results in elevated anxiety in mice, illustrating the heterogeneity of the brain reward circuit, and the complexity of nicotine dependence.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nguyen et al., 2021

claim: Nicotine inhibition of VTA dopamine neurons projecting to the amygdala results in elevated anxiety in mice.
source: An acute injection of nicotine also inhibits a subset of VTA dopamine neurons that project to the amygdala (Nguyen et al., 2021), and this results in elevated anxiety in mice, illustrating the heterogeneity of the brain reward circuit, and the complexity of nicotine dependence.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nguyen et al., 2021

claim: The medial habenulo-interpeduncular (MHb-IPN) axis is an important pathway in the neurobiology of nicotine addiction.
source: Another important pathway in the neurobiology of nicotine addiction is the medial habenulo-interpeduncular (MHb-IPN) axis (Fowler et al., 2011; Frahm et al., 2011; Molas et al., 2017; Morton et al., 2018; Tuesta et al., 2017; Wolfman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fowler et al., 2011; Frahm et al., 2011; Molas et al., 2017; Morton et al., 2018; Tuesta et al., 2017; Wolfman et al., 2018

claim: The MHb-IPN pathway is deeply implicated in the regulation of aversive physiological states such as fear and anxiety.
source: This pathway is deeply implicated in the regulation of aversive physiological states such as fear and anxiety (Molas et al., 2017; Otsu et al., 2019; Yamaguchi et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Molas et al., 2017; Otsu et al., 2019; Yamaguchi et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016

claim: The MHb-IPN pathway is believed to directly mediate aversion to high doses of nicotine.
source: It is believed to directly mediate aversion to high doses of nicotine (Fowler et al., 2011; Frahm et al., 2011), to trigger affective (anxiety) and somatic symptoms following nicotine withdrawal (Pang et al., 2016; Salas et al., 2009; Zhao-Shea et al., 2015; Zhao-Shea et al., 2013) and to be involved in relapse to nicotine-seeking (Forget et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fowler et al., 2011; Frahm et al., 2011

claim: The MHb-IPN pathway triggers affective and somatic symptoms following nicotine withdrawal.
source: It is believed to directly mediate aversion to high doses of nicotine (Fowler et al., 2011; Frahm et al., 2011), to trigger affective (anxiety) and somatic symptoms following nicotine withdrawal (Pang et al., 2016; Salas et al., 2009; Zhao-Shea et al., 2015; Zhao-Shea et al., 2013) and to be involved in relapse to nicotine-seeking (Forget et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pang et al., 2016; Salas et al., 2009; Zhao-Shea et al., 2015; Zhao-Shea et al., 2013

claim: The MHb-IPN pathway is involved in relapse to nicotine-seeking.
source: It is believed to directly mediate aversion to high doses of nicotine (Fowler et al., 2011; Frahm et al., 2011), to trigger affective (anxiety) and somatic symptoms following nicotine withdrawal (Pang et al., 2016; Salas et al., 2009; Zhao-Shea et al., 2015; Zhao-Shea et al., 2013) and to be involved in relapse to nicotine-seeking (Forget et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Forget et al., 2018

claim: Neurons of the MHb-IPN axis express the highest density and largest diversity of nAChRs in the brain.
source: Strikingly, neurons of the MHb-IPN axis express the highest density and largest diversity of nAChRs in the brain, notably the rare α5, α3, and β4 subunits (Zoli et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zoli et al., 2015

claim: The α5, α3, and β4 nAChR subunits are encoded by the CHRNA5-A3-B4 gene cluster.
source: These are encoded by the CHRNA5-A3-B4 gene cluster, some sequence variants of which are associated with a high risk of addiction in humans (Bierut et al., 2008; Lassi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bierut et al., 2008; Lassi et al., 2016

claim: Some sequence variants of the CHRNA5-A3-B4 gene cluster are associated with a high risk of addiction in humans.
source: These are encoded by the CHRNA5-A3-B4 gene cluster, some sequence variants of which are associated with a high risk of addiction in humans (Bierut et al., 2008; Lassi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bierut et al., 2008; Lassi et al., 2016

claim: The α3 and β4 subunits are virtually absent in the VTA or in other parts of the brain.
source: The α3 and β4 subunits are virtually absent in the VTA, or in other parts of the brain.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: About one-third to one-half of people who have tried smoking tobacco become regular users.
source: About one-third to one-half of people who have tried smoking tobacco become regular users (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2010

claim: Daily nicotine intake increased throughout the two-bottle choice paradigm, stabilizing at about 10 mg/kg/day on average for the highest nicotine concentration tested.
source: We found that daily nicotine intake increased throughout the paradigm, stabilizing at about 10 mg/kg/day on average for the highest nicotine concentration tested (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The percent of nicotine consumption was initially close to 50%, and decreased for nicotine concentrations above 50 μg/ml.
source: Overall, the percent of nicotine consumption, that is, the nicotine solution intake relative to the total fluid intake, was initially close to 50%, and decreased for nicotine concentrations above 50 μg/ml (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Mice responded rapidly (within a day) to the increase in nicotine concentration by adjusting their nicotine intake.
source: Indeed, we observed that mice responded rapidly (within a day) to the increase in nicotine concentration by adjusting their nicotine intake (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), resulting in titration of the nicotine dose, as previously reported (Fowler et al., 2011; Tuesta et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citations to Fowler et al., 2011; Tuesta et al., 2017

claim: About half of the WT mice (17/35) were classified as 'avoiders' who abruptly reduced their intake or had very low nicotine intake throughout the task.
source: In particular, some mice abruptly reduced their intake right after an increase in nicotine concentration in the bottle, or had very low nicotine intake throughout the task (intake never exceeded 2 mg/kg/day; Figure 1E). We classified these mice (17/35) as 'avoiders'.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: About half of the WT mice (18/35) were classified as 'non-avoiders' who displayed a continuous increase in nicotine intake or reached a titration plateau.
source: The other half of the mice (18/35), on the other hand, displayed a continuous increase in nicotine intake, or eventually reached a titration plateau in their consumption. These mice were classified as 'non-avoiders'.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Avoiders and non-avoiders showed similar nicotine intake for low concentrations of nicotine (10 and 50 µg/ml).
source: Avoiders and non-avoiders (phenotypes defined as above throughout the manuscript) showed on average similar nicotine intake for low concentrations of nicotine (10 and 50 µg/ml, p>0.05), but while nicotine intake increased throughout the task for non-avoiders (16.9±2.9 mg/kg/day for 200 μg/ml of nicotine) it dropped down to 2.6±0.4 mg/kg/day for such high nicotine concentration in avoiders (Figure 1F), and almost reached zero over the last 3 days (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F and 1G

claim: Nicotine intake increased throughout the task for non-avoiders to 16.9±2.9 mg/kg/day for 200 μg/ml of nicotine.
source: Avoiders and non-avoiders (phenotypes defined as above throughout the manuscript) showed on average similar nicotine intake for low concentrations of nicotine (10 and 50 µg/ml, p>0.05), but while nicotine intake increased throughout the task for non-avoiders (16.9±2.9 mg/kg/day for 200 μg/ml of nicotine) it dropped down to 2.6±0.4 mg/kg/day for such high nicotine concentration in avoiders (Figure 1F), and almost reached zero over the last 3 days (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F and 1G

claim: Nicotine intake dropped to 2.6±0.4 mg/kg/day for 200 μg/ml nicotine concentration in avoiders.
source: Avoiders and non-avoiders (phenotypes defined as above throughout the manuscript) showed on average similar nicotine intake for low concentrations of nicotine (10 and 50 µg/ml, p>0.05), but while nicotine intake increased throughout the task for non-avoiders (16.9±2.9 mg/kg/day for 200 μg/ml of nicotine) it dropped down to 2.6±0.4 mg/kg/day for such high nicotine concentration in avoiders (Figure 1F), and almost reached zero over the last 3 days (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F and 1G

claim: All naive mice actively avoided the quinine-containing solution and showed near-zero percent quinine consumption.
source: We found that all naive mice actively avoided the quinine-containing solution, and showed near-zero percent quinine consumption, as was observed with nicotine for avoiders, but not for non-avoiders (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Nicotine avoidance was not correlated with quinine avoidance.
source: We then used lower concentrations of quinine, and found that nicotine avoidance was not correlated with quinine avoidance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: Some non-avoiders actively tracked the side associated with nicotine when the bottles were swapped.
source: We found that some non-avoiders actively tracked the side associated with nicotine when the bottles were swapped (e.g. mouse #1 in Figure 2A), indicating a strong preference for the nicotine-containing bottle and active consumption.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Some non-avoiders displayed a strong side preference and never alternated drinking side.
source: Other non-avoiders displayed a strong side preference and never alternated drinking side (e.g. mouse #2 in Figure 2A), and hence consumed nicotine in a more passive fashion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: All avoider mice displayed active avoidance of the nicotine-containing solution.
source: In contrast, all avoider mice (n=17) displayed active avoidance of the nicotine-containing solution, whether they initially tracked the nicotine solution (e.g. mice #3 and 4 in Figure 2A) or not (e.g. mice #5 and 6 in Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The behavior of non-avoiders was fairly consistent throughout the task.
source: Overall, we found that the behavior of non-avoiders was on average fairly consistent throughout the task, that is their distance from the three apices was not really impacted by the modifications in nicotine concentration (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), whether they consumed nicotine actively or passively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: The behavior of avoiders was highly nicotine concentration-dependent.
source: In contrast, the behavior of avoiders was highly nicotine concentration-dependent, with mice going further away from the 100% nicotine apex as nicotine concentration increases (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: Aversion to nicotine in avoider mice mainly occurred at the transition from 100 to 200 μg/ml.
source: Aversion to nicotine in avoider mice mainly occurred at the transition from 100 to 200 μg/ml, but some mice displayed aversion at concentrations as low as 10 μg/ml (Figures 1E, 2A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E, 2A and C

claim: Some avoider mice displayed aversion at nicotine concentrations as low as 10 μg/ml.
source: Aversion to nicotine in avoider mice mainly occurred at the transition from 100 to 200 μg/ml, but some mice displayed aversion at concentrations as low as 10 μg/ml (Figures 1E, 2A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E, 2A and C

claim: Lowering nicotine concentration from 200 to 50 µg/ml did not increase percent nicotine consumption in avoiders.
source: Indeed, we found that lowering nicotine concentration from 200 to 50 µg/ml did not increase percent nicotine consumption in avoiders (Figure 2D), at least for the 4 days that mice were subjected to this concentration.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The amplitude of nicotine-evoked currents was higher in IPN neurons of avoider mice than in those from non-avoiders.
source: We found that the amplitude of nicotine-evoked currents was higher in IPN neurons of avoider mice than in those from non-avoiders (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: There was a negative correlation between the average amplitude of nicotine-evoked current in IPN neurons and nicotine consumption.
source: Specifically, there was a negative correlation between the average amplitude of nicotine-evoked current in IPN neurons, and nicotine consumption (measured over the last 24 hr prior to the patch-clamp recording, Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Prolonged exposure to nicotine reduced the amplitude of nicotine-evoked currents in the IPN compared to control mice treated with saline.
source: We then recorded from acute brain slices and found that indeed, prolonged exposure to nicotine reduced the amplitude of nicotine-evoked currents in the IPN of these mice compared to control mice treated with saline (Figure 3A; no anatomical sampling bias between the two groups, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Nicotine i.v. injections in naive WT mice induce an increase in the firing rate of IPN neurons compared with saline injection.
source: We found that nicotine i.v. injections in naive WT mice induce an increase in the firing rate of IPN neurons compared with saline injection, and that this acute effect of nicotine was reduced after the prolonged (4 weeks) passive exposure of the mice to the drug (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The acute effect of nicotine on IPN neuron firing rate was reduced after prolonged (4 weeks) passive exposure to the drug.
source: We found that nicotine i.v. injections in naive WT mice induce an increase in the firing rate of IPN neurons compared with saline injection, and that this acute effect of nicotine was reduced after the prolonged (4 weeks) passive exposure of the mice to the drug (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The amplitude of the response to nicotine in IPN neurons was positively correlated with spontaneous activity.
source: In both nicotine- and saline-treated animals, the amplitude of the response to nicotine was positively correlated with spontaneous activity: neurons with high basal activity responded to nicotine with a greater change in firing frequency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G

claim: Mice pretreated with saline avoided nicotine at 100 µg/ml concentration.
source: We found that mice pretreated with saline (controls) avoided nicotine (Figure 3C), which may indicate aversion to such high nicotine concentration.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Mice pretreated with nicotine did not avoid nicotine at 100 µg/ml concentration.
source: In contrast, mice pretreated with nicotine did not avoid nicotine, suggesting that they may have developed a tolerance for the aversive effects of the drug.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Nicotine consumption was greater in the nicotine-treated group than in the saline-treated group.
source: Overall, nicotine consumption was greater in the nicotine-treated group than in the saline-treated group (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Chrnb4-/- mice displayed both greater percent nicotine consumption and nicotine intake than WT animals.
source: We found that Chrnb4-/- mice displayed both greater percent nicotine consumption and nicotine intake than WT animals, with minimal concentration-dependent change in percent nicotine consumption (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: None of the Chrnb4-/- mice (0/13) showed aversion-like behavior at high nicotine concentration.
source: Strikingly, however, none of the Chrnb4-/- mice (0/13) showed aversion-like behavior at high nicotine concentration, which contrasts with the high proportion of avoiders in WT animals (17/35, Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, P=0.04 Pearson's Chi squared with Yates' continuity correction).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Avoidance to quinine was similar in WT and Chrnb4-/- mice.
source: Avoidance to quinine was similar in WT and Chrnb4-/- mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), further suggesting that avoidance to nicotine is not linked to different sensitivities to the bitterness of nicotine.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: The amplitude of nicotine-evoked currents in the IPN was on average three-fold lower in Chrnb4-/- than in WT mice.
source: We found that the amplitude of nicotine-evoked currents in the IPN was on average three-fold lower in Chrnb4-/- than in WT mice (Figure 4D), confirming that β4-containing (β4*) nAChRs are the major receptor subtype in the rostral IPN.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: β4-containing nAChRs are the major receptor subtype in the rostral IPN.
source: We found that the amplitude of nicotine-evoked currents in the IPN was on average three-fold lower in Chrnb4-/- than in WT mice (Figure 4D), confirming that β4-containing (β4*) nAChRs are the major receptor subtype in the rostral IPN.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and inference from the comparison

claim: Prolonged nicotine treatment had no significant effect on the amplitude of nAChR currents in Chrnb4-/- mice.
source: We also found that prolonged nicotine treatment had no significant effect on the amplitude of nAChR currents in these knock-out mice (Figure 4D), suggesting that the downregulation observed after chronic nicotine treatment in the IPN of WT mice mainly affects β4*nAChRs (and not other subtypes such as β2*nAChRs for instance).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The downregulation observed after chronic nicotine treatment in the IPN of WT mice mainly affects β4*nAChRs.
source: We also found that prolonged nicotine treatment had no significant effect on the amplitude of nAChR currents in these knock-out mice (Figure 4D), suggesting that the downregulation observed after chronic nicotine treatment in the IPN of WT mice mainly affects β4*nAChRs (and not other subtypes such as β2*nAChRs for instance).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect in Chrnb4-/- mice

claim: Nicotine i.v. injections resulted in an increase in IPN neuron activity that was larger in WT mice than in Chrnb4-/- mice.
source: Nicotine i.v. injections (30 μg/kg) resulted in an increase in IPN neuron activity (Figure 4E), that was larger in WT mice than in Chrnb4-/- mice, further demonstrating the important role of β4*nAChRs in the response of the IPN to nicotine.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: β4*nAChRs play an important role in the response of the IPN to nicotine.
source: Nicotine i.v. injections (30 μg/kg) resulted in an increase in IPN neuron activity (Figure 4E), that was larger in WT mice than in Chrnb4-/- mice, further demonstrating the important role of β4*nAChRs in the response of the IPN to nicotine.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison between WT and Chrnb4-/- mice

claim: β4*nAChRs play little role in regulating the excitability of IPN neurons in anesthetized mice.
source: Overall, IPN neurons of WT and Chrnb4-/- mice had similar spontaneous frequencies (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E), suggesting that β4*nAChRs play little role in regulating the excitability of IPN neurons in anesthetized mice.
evidence: Inferred from the similar spontaneous frequencies in WT and Chrnb4-/- mice

claim: β4*nAChRs are mainly involved in increasing, not decreasing, neuronal activity in response to nicotine injection.
source: In both WT and Chrnb4-/- mice, we observed a population of neurons that decreased their firing rate, but with no difference in response amplitude between the two genotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G), suggesting that β4*nAChR are mainly involved in increasing, not decreasing, neuronal activity in response to nicotine injection.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of difference between genotypes in nicotine-inhibited neurons

claim: Transduction of β4 in the IPN increased the amplitude of nicotine-evoked currents.
source: Transduction of β4, but not of GFP alone, in the IPN increased the amplitude of nicotine-evoked currents (Figure 5B) and restored levels found in WT animals (U test, p=0.6, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Transduction of β4 in the IPN restored nicotine-evoked current levels to those found in WT animals.
source: Transduction of β4, but not of GFP alone, in the IPN increased the amplitude of nicotine-evoked currents (Figure 5B) and restored levels found in WT animals (U test, p=0.6, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Transduction of β4 in the IPN restored the response to nicotine in vivo.
source: Transduction of β4 in the IPN also restored the response to nicotine in vivo (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Re-expression of β4 in the IPN of Chrnb4-/- mice decreased nicotine intake compared to the group of mice transduced with eGFP in the IPN.
source: We found that re-expression of β4 in the IPN of Chrnb4-/- mice decreased nicotine intake compared to the group of mice transduced with eGFP in the IPN (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Nicotine intake was similar in WT and in KO-β4IPN animals.
source: Overall, nicotine intake was similar in WT and in KO-β4IPN animals (p>0.5 for all concentrations), demonstrating the causal role of β4 nAChRs of IPN neurons in nicotine consumption behaviors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The proportion of mice that avoided nicotine at 200 μg/kg was very low for KO-GFPIPN control mice (2/18), but greater for KO-β4IPN mice (8/17).
source: At the individual level, the proportion mice that avoided nicotine at 200 μg/kg was very low for KO-GFPIPN control mice (2/18), but greater for KO-β4IPN mice (8/17, Figure 5E, p=0.04 Chi squared).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Selective re-expression of β4 in the IPN of Chrnb4-/- mice rescued aversion for nicotine.
source: Collectively, these results show that selective re-expression of β4 in the IPN of Chrnb4-/- mice rescued aversion for nicotine, and highlight the specific role of IPN β4*nAChRs in signaling aversion to nicotine, and in the control of nicotine intake.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results

claim: IPN β4*nAChRs play a specific role in signaling aversion to nicotine and in the control of nicotine intake.
source: Collectively, these results show that selective re-expression of β4 in the IPN of Chrnb4-/- mice rescued aversion for nicotine, and highlight the specific role of IPN β4*nAChRs in signaling aversion to nicotine, and in the control of nicotine intake.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results

claim: The functional expression level of β4-containing nAChRs in the IPN underlies different sensitivities to the aversive properties of nicotine.
source: We also found that the functional expression level of β4-containing nAChRs in the IPN underlies these different sensitivities to the aversive properties of nicotine.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results

claim: Long-term exposure to nicotine decreases the likelihood to reach the threshold at which mice develop aversion to the drug.
source: We suggest that long-term exposure to nicotine decreases the likelihood to reach the threshold at which mice develop aversion to the drug, which ultimately leads to increased drug consumption.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results

claim: Nicotine intake history weakens the ability of nicotine to induce aversion in mice.
source: In other words, nicotine intake history weakens the ability of nicotine to induce aversion in mice.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results

claim: Mice under prolonged nicotine administration develop tolerance to the aversive effects of nicotine.
source: However, our data indicate that mice under prolonged nicotine administration will also develop tolerance to the aversive effects of nicotine, underscoring the necessity to develop alternative medical approaches.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results

claim: β4-containing nAChRs, by engaging the IPN circuitry, initiate a primary response to nicotine that, if above a certain threshold, will trigger acute aversion to the drug.
source: We suggest that β4-containing nAChRs, by engaging the IPN circuitry, initiate a primary response to nicotine that, if above a certain threshold, will trigger acute aversion to the drug, impacting the balance between drug reward and aversion to limit drug consumption.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the experimental results

claim: Pharmacological or optogenetic stimulation of the MHb-IPN pathway directly produces aversion.
source: Consistent with this, pharmacological or optogenetic stimulation of the MHb-IPN pathway directly produces aversion (Morton et al., 2018; Tuesta et al., 2017; Wolfman et al., 2018), while pharmacological inactivation of this pathway increases nicotine intake (Fowler et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morton et al., 2018; Tuesta et al., 2017; Wolfman et al., 2018; Fowler et al., 2011

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of the MHb-IPN pathway increases nicotine intake.
source: Consistent with this, pharmacological or optogenetic stimulation of the MHb-IPN pathway directly produces aversion (Morton et al., 2018; Tuesta et al., 2017; Wolfman et al., 2018), while pharmacological inactivation of this pathway increases nicotine intake (Fowler et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fowler et al., 2011

claim: An initial unpleasant reaction to cigarettes is associated with a reduced likelihood of continued smoking in humans.
source: This is consistent with findings in humans, where an initial unpleasant reaction to cigarettes is associated with a reduced likelihood of continued smoking (DiFranza et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to DiFranza et al., 2004

claim: Prolonged nicotine exposure downregulated and/or desensitized β4-containing nAChRs of the IPN.
source: Indeed, we discovered that prolonged nicotine exposure downregulated and/or desensitized β4-containing nAChRs of the IPN, as evidenced by the decreased response to nicotine both ex vivo and in vivo, and the absence of effect in Chrnb4-/- mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ex vivo and in vivo recordings

claim: Chronic nicotine causes functional upregulation of nicotinic currents in MHb neurons of mice.
source: Chronic nicotine was shown to cause functional upregulation of nicotinic currents in MHb neurons of mice (Arvin et al., 2019; Banala et al., 2018; Pang et al., 2016; Shih et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2020) and rats (Jin et al., 2020), as well as in IPN neurons of mice (Zhao-Shea et al., 2013) and rats (Tapia et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arvin et al., 2019; Banala et al., 2018; Pang et al., 2016; Shih et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2020; Zhao-Shea et al., 2013; Tapia et al., 2022

claim: Upregulation of nAChRs is highly cell-type as well as receptor-subtype dependent.
source: However, it should be noted that upregulation is highly cell-type as well as receptor-subtype dependent (Nashmi et al., 2007; Shih et al., 2015; Zhao-Shea et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nashmi et al., 2007; Shih et al., 2015; Zhao-Shea et al., 2013

claim: In cell culture, β2-, but not β4-containing nAChRs were upregulated after nicotine treatment.
source: Moreover, in cell culture, it was found that β2-, but not β4-containing nAChRs were upregulated after nicotine treatment (Wang et al., 1998), which agrees with our findings.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 1998
